headline: Texas Democrats file bills to legalize marijuana for the 2027 session
dek: Texas House Democrats filed HB 369 and HB 362 on 9 November to legalize adult-use cannabis with 12-plant home grow and a 15% plus 20% tax stack.
key_points: HB 369 (Rep. Joe Moody) and HB 362 (Rep. John Bucy III) would let adults 21+ possess 2 ounces and grow 12 plants, with licensed sales.
The House bills tax cultivator-to-store transfers at 15% and retail sales at 20%, on top of sales tax; SB 237 in the Senate relies on fees instead.
Other prefiled bills would cut concentrate penalties, add menstrual conditions to the medical programme and bar most public-sector cannabis drug testing.
Democrats now hold statewide offices and a House majority, but leaders disagree on full legalization, medical expansion or a voter referendum.
body: Texas lawmakers have begun prefiling cannabis legalization bills for the 2027 session, one week after the midterm elections put Democrats in control of the state's top offices and the House of Representatives. Rep. Joe Moody filed HB 369, titled the Texas Regulation of Cannabis Act, on Monday 9 November, according to the Texas Legislature's own records, and Rep. John Bucy III filed HB 362 with largely identical provisions, Marijuana Moment reported.

Both House bills would let adults aged 21 and over possess, use and transport up to 2 ounces of cannabis, including no more than 15 grams of concentrate, and grow up to 12 plants at home. They would also create a licensed market covering cultivation, processing, transport, testing and retail. A Senate companion of sorts, SB 237 from Sen. Carol Alvarado, takes a looser approach on possession and a lighter approach on tax.
## What the House bills would build

Under HB 369 and HB 362, the Texas Commission of Licensing and Regulation would write the rules and the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation would run the programme, putting cannabis in the same agency that licenses dozens of other trades rather than creating a new regulator. Local governments would not be able to ban cannabis businesses or restrict them unreasonably, according to Marijuana Moment's summary.

The tax design is two-layered. Transfers from cultivators to dispensaries would be taxed at 15%, and retail sales would carry a further 20% at the till, in addition to ordinary sales tax. Revenue would be split 50% to schools, 25% to a veterans' assistance fund, 15% to drug treatment and 10% to local governments.
> Texas Democrats now have the offices to move a cannabis bill. What they do not yet have is one answer to what the bill should be.

Alvarado's SB 237 follows a similar framework but differs on three points that matter to operators. It sets a higher possession limit of 2.5 ounces. It lets counties ban cannabis businesses, the opposite of the House bills' local protection. And it imposes no new excise tax, raising money instead through licence and application fees.

For investors, the gap between those models is large. A market built on the House bills would stack a 15% wholesale-stage tax and a 20% retail tax before sales tax; for comparison, Connecticut's adult-use purchases now carry about 20.1% in total after the state replaced its THC-based tax with a flat 10.75% gross receipts tax on 1 October, according to Paybotic's summary of state data. A fee-only model would leave far more room on price against the illicit market and the hemp shops that have served Texas consumers until now, but less revenue for the causes the House bills earmark.
## The rest of the prefiled package

Other cannabis bills filed for the session that begins in January include HB 667 from Moody, which would generally lower penalties for marijuana concentrates; HB 330 from Rep. Mihaela Plesa, which would add conditions causing menstrual cramps, including premenstrual dysphoric disorder and dysmenorrhea, to the medical programme; and HB 507 from Bucy, which would stop state agencies and local governments from drug testing most employees and contractors for cannabinoids or penalising them for lawful use of low-THC medical cannabis or consumable hemp, Marijuana Moment reported.

The bills arrive before the incoming leadership has picked a path. As we reported this morning, Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin has said there are differing views even within the industry on whether to expand the Texas Compassionate Use Program or legalize outright. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she wants voters to decide through a legislative referendum, which under Texas law would have to take the form of a constitutional amendment.

Goodwin has also said she opposes a hemp THC ban and wants the Department of State Health Services to unwind the restrictive hemp rules it adopted after Gov. Greg Abbott vetoed the legislature's ban, rules now being challenged in court. That fight runs alongside the federal hemp THC limit due on 11 December, which would hit Texas's hemp retailers regardless of what Austin decides.

Local voters have moved already: Houston approved a ballot measure last week making misdemeanor marijuana possession the lowest enforcement priority for police, Marijuana Moment reported. Texas remains a state with no adult-use law and only a limited medical programme, according to MetaFlora's Texas legal hub.

Before the session opens in January, watch for a Senate bill closer to the House model and for any Republican cosponsors, a sign of whether a bill could survive a floor vote. Watch how Goodwin, as lieutenant governor, handles the Senate side, and whether Hinojosa's referendum idea turns into a joint resolution. On hemp, 11 December brings the federal limit and the state's court fight over DSHS rules continues.
